backTranslations.41:
**Before the appointment**
- Add the appointment date in the Visit tab. MenoMap shows you how ready your notes are and what would make them more complete.
- Choose the topics and questions that matter most to you. Limit yourself to three or four.
- Create your notes for the last 30 or 90 days. Check that your medication list is up to date.

**During the appointment**
- Hand over or show the first page. It is designed to be read in under a minute: counts, averages, the heat calendar and your questions.
- Start with the question that matters most to you.
- If your health professional speaks another language, you can create the notes in that language.

**What the notes are and are not**

They are a summary of what you logged, plus whatever you decided to bring from the Health app. They are not a diagnosis or a complete medical record, and any pattern that appears in them is a coincidence check, not proof of the cause. Your health professional may ask questions the notes cannot answer, and that is normal.

**After the appointment**

Add any new medication with its start date. In a few weeks, MenoMap can show you your before and after records, which makes your next review easier.
backTranslations.42:
**Menopause** is a single point in time: the day when 12 months in a row without a period have passed, when that is not explained by something else (such as pregnancy, some medications or surgery). In many countries it happens on average in the early 50s, but it is common at any time between the mid 40s and mid 50s.

**Perimenopause** is the period of years leading up to that moment. Hormone levels rise and fall unevenly, so periods can become irregular, heavier, lighter, more frequent or more spread out. Many of the changes associated with menopause, such as hot flashes, night sweats and changes in sleep and mood, usually begin in this stage, while there are still periods. Perimenopause can last a few years or quite a bit longer, and it is different for each person.

**Postmenopause** is everything that comes after that 12-month mark. Some symptoms calm down over time; others can continue for years.

Menopause can also come earlier because of surgery in which the ovaries are removed, some cancer treatments or other health problems. Menopause before age 40 is sometimes called premature ovarian insufficiency, and it is worth discussing with a health professional.

**How it is recognized.** In many people over 45, health professionals recognize perimenopause or menopause from your history and symptoms. Blood tests are not always needed, because hormone levels change from one day to the next. They are more likely to be used when the person is younger or the picture is unclear.

**What MenoMap does and does not do.** MenoMap cannot tell you what stage you are in. What it can do is keep an honest record of what you notice: surges, sleep, mood and treatment, so that you and your health professional can see the same picture.

backTranslations.162:
Health professionals call hot flashes and night sweats **vasomotor symptoms**. A hot flash is a sudden wave of heat, often in the face, neck and chest, sometimes with flushing, sweating, a racing heart or a chill afterward. A night sweat is the same thing during sleep, and it can be strong enough to wake you or soak your sheets.

They are among the most common changes around menopause. Some people have a few mild ones; others have many a day, interrupting their work and sleep. In some they go away within a few years; in others they last much longer.

**What can make them more likely.** Many people notice patterns with alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, hot places, stress or heavy bedding. This varies a lot from person to person, which is why logging your own tags can be more useful than a general list.

**There are other causes.** Flushing and sweating can also be due to thyroid problems, infections, some medications, anxiety and other conditions. If your symptoms don't fit the usual pattern, or come with weight loss, fever or feeling unwell, talk about it with a health professional.

**How to describe them well.** Details that are useful for an appointment:
- How many you have per day and at night, roughly
- How strong they feel and how long they last
- What they interrupt: sleep, work, conversations, exercise
- What seems to happen before they appear
- What you have tried and whether anything changed

MenoMap's Surge button and the log afterward exist precisely to capture this without much effort.

**Help is available.** There are hormonal and non-hormonal treatment options, as well as practical approaches. Which are right for you is something worth discussing with a health professional.

backTranslations.291:
Hormone therapy (often called HRT or MHT) replaces some of the estrogen the body produces less of around menopause. The main guidelines describe it as an effective treatment for hot flashes and night sweats in many people, and it can also help with other symptoms.

**It comes in different forms:** patches, gels, sprays, tablets and low-dose vaginal products for local symptoms such as dryness. People who still have a uterus are normally prescribed a progestogen together with the estrogen to protect the lining of the uterus.

**Benefits and risks depend on each person:** age, time since periods stopped, personal and family history (for example, of breast cancer, clots, stroke or heart disease), and the type and route of treatment. That is why it is a decision made with a health professional who knows your history, not something an app can decide.

**Questions people often ask:**
- Is hormone therapy an option for me, and why or why not?
- What type and form would you suggest for me, and why?
- What benefits could I expect, and how soon?
- What are my personal risks, and how do they compare with not treating?
- What should I watch for, and when should it be reviewed?

**If you already use it,** log it in MenoMap (You → Medications). MenoMap will show you your surges before and after you started, as a coincidence check and not proof, so you have something concrete to discuss at the review.

MenoMap never suggests starting, stopping or changing a medication.

backTranslations.293:
Hormone therapy is not suitable for everyone, and some people simply prefer other paths. There are several.

**Prescription options.** Some non-hormonal medications have evidence that they reduce hot flashes. They include certain medications originally created for other conditions and a newer class designed specifically for hot flashes. Each has its own benefits, side effects and interactions, so a health professional can help you weigh them.

**Psychological therapy and mind-body approaches.** Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) adapted to menopause has evidence that it makes hot flashes and night sweats less bothersome and improves sleep. Clinical hypnosis has also been studied.

**Practical changes that help many people:**
- Layers of clothing you can take off quickly
- A fan on your desk and next to the bed
- A cooler bedroom and breathable bedding
- Noticing and reducing your own triggers (MenoMap's tags and experiments help with this)
- Regular physical activity and a stable sleep routine

**Supplements and herbal products.** The evidence is mixed or limited for many of them, quality varies and some interact with other medications. Tell your health professional or your pharmacist everything you take, including over-the-counter products.

**Try one change at a time.** MenoMap's two-week experiments compare your own logs before and during a change, which is easier to assess than a feeling.

backTranslations.416:
Most appointments are short, and it's hard to remember a month of nights in the moment. We tend to remember the most recent days or the worst ones. A simple log fills that gap.

**What a diary gives your health professional:**
- How often symptoms appear and how strong they are, not just that they appear
- Whether things are getting better, worse or staying the same
- What was going on around them: sleep, alcohol, stress, medications
- A starting point for comparison if you try a treatment

**Keep it light.** A diary only helps if you keep it up. MenoMap is built around a one-tap Surge button and a four-question review of the night, so it takes seconds, not a notebook.

**Two weeks is a good start.** Two to four weeks of logs usually show a clearer picture than a single bad week.

**Bring your questions too.** Write down what matters most to you: the symptom that bothers you most, what you want to try or avoid, and anything that worries you. MenoMap's Visit tab helps you choose questions and prints them with your notes.

backTranslations.479:
Once 12 months have passed without a period, **any vaginal bleeding should be checked by a health professional**, even if it happened only once, and even if it was only spotting or a light pink or brown discharge.

Most of the time, the cause turns out not to be serious. For example, thinning of the lining of the vagina or uterus is common. But bleeding after menopause can sometimes be an early sign of a condition that is much easier to treat if caught early. That is why public health recommendations say to have it checked rather than wait.

**If you use hormone therapy,** some bleeding patterns may be expected, depending on the type you use. Bleeding that is unexpected for your treatment, heavier than usual or that happens at a time that doesn't fit should also be checked.

**What to do:**
- Contact your health professional or your health service and say that you had bleeding after menopause.
- Note the date, the amount and anything else you noticed. MenoMap can save it for you (You → Cycle).

MenoMap cannot tell you why the bleeding happened. It will remind you to have it checked and will include it in your notes for the appointment.

backTranslations.529:
Sleeping badly is one of the most common troubles in midlife, and it rarely has a single cause.

**Night sweats** can wake you directly, or leave you too hot or damp to get back to sleep.

**Other common factors:**
- Needing to urinate at night
- Anxiety or a racing mind
- Alcohol, which can help you fall asleep but often fragments the second half of the night
- Caffeine later in the day
- Pain, restless legs or your partner's snoring
- Snoring or pauses in breathing, which can be a sign of sleep apnea (worth mentioning, especially if you are very sleepy during the day)

**What usually helps.** A cool, dark room; breathable bedding and layered clothing you can take off; a fixed wake-up time; and less alcohol near bedtime. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured, well-studied approach, and many health professionals can point you toward it.

**What to log.** For a week or two, note your sleep score, night surges, alcohol and late caffeine. MenoMap's night review and surge log do it in a few taps. If you use an Apple Watch, MenoMap can show your sleep and wrist temperature from the Health app next to your night sweats, as context and not as an explanation.

**When to see someone.** Talk to a health professional if sleeping badly affects your safety (for example, when driving), your mood or your daily life, or if you notice pauses in your breathing or gasping during the night.
